newsitem.title: UK: Cloning offers hope, not threats - fertility expert.
newsitem.headline: Cloning offers hope, not threats - fertility expert.

text.p: Cloning offers hope and opportunities for medicine, not a moral threat, Lord Robert Winston, who helped pioneer test-tube fertilisation, said on Friday.
Winston criticised "knee-jerk" reaction against the news that scientists in Scotland had cloned an adult sheep for the first time, pointing out the potential for human medicine.
"The production of Dolly should not be seen as a moral threat, but rather as an exciting challenge," he wrote in a commentary for the British Medical Journal.
"To answer this good science with a knee-jerk political reaction, as did (U.S.) President Clinton recently, shows poor judgment."

When news of Dolly's successful birth splashed across front pages several weeks ago, Clinton tightened bans on the use of federal funds for cloning research and urged a special panel to study the implications.
Similar reactions came from the Vatican, the European Union, and many governments.
Winston, now lauded as Britain's leading expert on test-tube fertilisation, said people were ignoring the potential benefits offered by cloning technology.
"In a society which is still scientifically illiterate, the onus is on researchers to explain the potential good that can be gained in the laboratory," he wrote.

For instance, few had pointed out that Dolly was not 100 percent a clone, he said. Created by injecting the nucleus from an adult sheep cell into the egg cell of a second ewe, Dolly had most of the genetic make-up of the first sheep.
But her mitochondrial DNA came from the egg donor. Mitochondrial DNA lies outside the nucleus and is passed down, unchanged except for accidental mutation, from mother to child.
DNA in the nucleus is a mixture from the mother and father.
Mitochondrial DNA was used to verify the remains of Russia's Tsar Nicholas II and his family, killed in 1918, and is used by scientists to trace the genetic origins of the human race.

"Mitochondria are important in the aging process because aging is related to acquired mutations in mitochondrial DNA, possibly caused by oxygen damage during an individual's life," Winston wrote. This needed study, he said.
Banning cloning techniques could close doors to some infertile couples desperate for children, Winston added.

Winston himself is one of the few doctors legally authorised to perform sex-selection. He helped develop a technique for identifying the sex of an embryo before it is taken from a test-tube and implanted in the mother.
This helps prevent the birth of children with sex-linked disorders such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a wasting disorder affecting only boys, or haemophilia.
"Self-regulation and legislation already work well," he said.
